question: What happens to the solid particles in a drug suspension over time?

options.A: Solid particles are dispersed and tend to settle
options.B: Solid particles are fully dissolved in the liquid
options.C: Active ingredients are bound permanently to the bottle
options.D: The mixture remains completely clear at all times

explanation: Think of muddy water! Suspensions have tiny bits of medicine floating around that love to sink to the bottom if left alone. That's why we always shake them first!

question: Why is it risky to give a patient an unmixed suspension right from the bottle?

options.A: The liquid will foam up and block the patient's airway
options.B: The patient might get a weak dose first and a toxic dose last
options.C: The medicine will taste too sweet and cause vomiting
options.D: The solid particles will react chemically with stomach acid

explanation: Spot on! Since the medicine settles at the bottom, an unmixed bottle means watery liquid at first (weak dose) and a sludgy finish at the end (too strong!).

question: When giving a thick oral suspension through a feeding tube, why do we dilute it first?

options.A: To make the medication taste much sweeter
options.B: To destroy harmful bacteria growing in the liquid
options.C: To prevent the thick liquid from clogging the tube
options.D: To speed up how fast the drug enters the bloodstream

explanation: You got it! Thick syrups and suspensions love to gum up feeding tubes. Diluting keeps everything flowing smoothly so the patient gets their full feed and meds.

question: How does diluting a medication help when giving tiny doses to an infant?

options.A: It completely eliminates all potential drug side effects
options.B: It makes measuring a larger volume more accurate
options.C: It prevents the infant from developing a drug allergy
options.D: It shortens the half-life of the drug in the body

explanation: Measuring tiny drops like 0.2 mL can be nerve-wracking. Diluting lets you draw up a slightly bigger, much safer-to-measure amount!

question: What is an essential safety habit after calculating a children's drug dose?

options.A: Throw away half of the calculated medication
options.B: Heat the liquid to body temperature before giving
options.C: Ask another nurse to double-check the math
options.D: Store the leftover mixture in a dark refrigerator

explanation: Two pairs of eyes are always better than one, especially with kids' doses! A quick double-check keeps everyone safe and builds your clinical confidence.

question: A doctor orders 250 mg of a suspension. The bottle label says 125 mg per 5 mL. How much should you measure?
explanation: Nice calculation! Dose ordered (250) divided by stock dose (125) equals 2. Multiply that by 5 mL, and you get 10 mL. You're getting the hang of this!

question: What is the very first thing you should do before preparing to measure a medication?

options.A: Shake the empty measuring cup vigorously
options.B: Pour the medication directly down the drain
options.C: Heat the glass bottle in a microwave oven
options.D: Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves

explanation: Safety first! Standard infection control always starts with clean hands before touching any patient supplies or medications.

question: Why must you shake a suspension bottle vigorously right before pouring a dose?

options.A: To cool down the liquid inside the glass container
options.B: To evenly redistribute settled solid drug particles
options.C: To check if the outer safety seal is broken
options.D: To create air bubbles that make the drug taste better

explanation: Shaking mixes the active medicine back into the liquid so the patient gets the right dose, not just flavored water!

question: Which of these habits helps keep oral syringes clean and free of germs?

options.A: Rinsing the dirty syringe in a shared sink basin
options.B: Storing open syringes in a warm pocket all day
options.C: Avoiding touching the syringe tip to any surface
options.D: Touching the tip directly to the patient's tongue

explanation: Keep that tip sterile! Touching it to counters or fingers can introduce unwanted bacteria right back into the medicine bottle.

question: What can happen if you mix certain suspensions with the wrong type of liquid?

options.A: The liquid immediately changes into a bright gas
options.B: The drug becomes twice as potent instantly
options.C: The active drug may precipitate or break down
options.D: The medication turns into a solid plastic block

explanation: Chemical reactions can ruin a drug! Mixing incompatible fluids can cause the medicine to clump up, fall apart, or lose its healing power.

question: What key tip should you teach a mother giving an oral suspension to her toddler at home?

options.A: Store the open bottle on a sunny kitchen windowsill
options.B: Shake the bottle well immediately before every single dose
options.C: Mix the entire bottle with juice and keep it on the counter
options.D: Stop the medication as soon as the child feels better

explanation: Empowering mothers with good education is key! Reminding them to shake the bottle every time ensures the child gets the exact medicine they need.

question: Where is the safest place in an infant's mouth to squirt liquid medication?

options.A: Between the infant's cheek and gum in the side of the mouth
options.B: Underneath the infant's tongue like a sublingual tablet
options.C: Mixed into a large bowl of hot porridge for breakfast
options.D: Directly down the center of the infant's throat

explanation: Smart nursing trick! Pushing liquid into the side of the cheek prevents choking and gagging, making medicine time much calmer for baby and nurse.

question: What crucial detail must you write on a newly mixed (reconstituted) suspension bottle?

options.A: The patient's room number and diagnosis
options.B: The exact date and time the medication expires
options.C: The name of the pharmacy supplier

explanation: Always label your mixtures! Reconstituted drugs spoil fast once water is added, so tracking the expiry date keeps your patient safe.

question: Why do freshly mixed (reconstituted) suspensions expire much faster than dry powders?

options.A: The active drug evaporates into the air inside the room
options.B: The plastic bottle begins to melt in the refrigerator
options.C: Water activates chemical breakdown and microbial growth
options.D: Refrigeration destroys the chemical bonds of the powder

explanation: Water wakes everything up! Once water is added, it triggers chemical breakdown and creates a cozy home for bacteria to multiply. That's why they don't last long.
